newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says Italy needs German confidence for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says Italy needs German confidence for EMU.

text.p: Italy expects no "discount" from Germany for its entry into the single European currency from the start but needs to win the confidence of the German people, Prime Minister Roman Prodi was quoted as saying on Wednesday.

Prodi was speaking in an interview with the Milan daily Corriere della Sera published the day before the Dublin summit of European Union (EU) finance ministers was expected to focus on the Economica and Monetary Union budget pact.

He said Italy's tough 1997 draft budget, due to be appproved by parliament by the end of this month, aimed to achieve the Maastricht parameter of a deficit/gross domestic product (GDP) ratio of 3.0 percent.

But he said "I know the European situation too well not to be aware that if at the time of the examination (of Maastricht criteria) France is at 3.3 percent and Italy at 3.32 percent, they will enter and we won't.

"Because 1998 will be an election year in Germany, the problem Italy faces is that of German public opinion," he said. "For them, we are traditionally bearers of instability and inflation, and it is clear that Germany will not want nor will be able to give us any discount."

As a result, Prodi said Italy must "turn up for the appointment with our numbers perfectly in order, possibly 0.1-percent below the criteria but certainly not 0.1-percent above them. Furthermore, it certainly won't be Italy asking for interpretative revisions or any delays.
"My goal must be to present myself to the other nations with two years of virtuous behaviour behind me which can convince even German public opinion. I have no other choice," he said.

Asked if the lira's return to the European currency grid marked a closer relationship between France and Italy, Prodi said "as long as this is not considered to be anti-German then, the answer is yes."

He said 1998 was also likely to be an election year for France. "But the difference with Germany is that no French elector would reproach (President Jacques) Chirac for having supported Italy's entry."

Asked why he had ruled out a "mini-budget" to make sure Italy's finances were in order next year, as deemed necessary by many respected economists, Prodi said his forecast for Italian growth differed from that of some of his colleagues. "But we will see," he added.
